name: Aisha Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the water and drainage crew at Blue Mesa, a large open pit mine, and operate the heavy pump truck myself. We keep rainwater from flooding the digging benches and check the pipe joints before a storm. My two-year technical diploma taught me the calculations, but I also know where water will collect from walking the pit. I like solving a practical problem; midnight callouts wear me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the job support outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, and my husband Victor and I have grown children who live elsewhere. He works at a clinic, so his pay does not depend on the mine, and we have more than nine months of expenses saved. My mine wage is high for this role, with several similar jobs at other pits nearby. I hope to leave regular shifts around 65 if the retirement account supports it. I use an AI assistant now and then to compare rainfall tables, after a colleague showed me how to verify its sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a faster rainfall table is useful if the pump test is still done beside the pipe. I would use a tool that saves time, after checking the sums. A wet bench does not care how smart the report sounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The work and pay look secure, and Victor's clinic wage gives us a second source of income. I would feel no pressure to change jobs. I could use the assistant for rain tables occasionally while keeping the physical pump checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the pump truck roster and compare any AI rainfall summary with the gauge record each week. I'd continue our scheduled retirement transfers and renew the oldest pipe joint this winter. In the first year I'd show the crew which table errors I found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The day would still have its rain and repairs, but the household could manage them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error do you find most often?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A missing gauge reading can make one day look dry when the pit was soaked. I circle the blank cell and go to the original log. The pump still has to be ready for real water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children hear about the software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if one of my grown children asked about work. They know I check numbers twice. I would rather tell them about the new pipe joint than a report shortcut.

say: I would use **faster rain tables** after comparing them with gauge readings.
I would tell the crew the **physical pump test** remains essential.
think: The **mine wage** and Victor’s separate clinic pay make our household secure.
I could keep **occasional AI use** without changing the work I enjoy.
do: Keep the **pump roster** and compare rainfall summaries with gauge logs weekly.
Renew the **oldest pipe joint** this winter and show the crew any table errors.
S0.quote: A wet bench does not care how smart the report sounds.
fieldNote: Her **test habit** checks the original rainfall log before trusting a summary.
Her **strong reserve** and a second income make ordinary repairs manageable without forcing a change of job or household plans.

steps.text: Keep running the Blue Mesa pump truck and checking rainfall logs
Renew the oldest pump pipe joint this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can order pipe and plan callouts sooner than a robot can fit a joint on a muddy bench. I would ask for a measured trial of any remote pump. If it holds through a storm, I would consider using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ordering part of my lead role may shrink, and a remote pump could eventually reduce callouts. I might lose some hours, although I have other pits within reach and Victor's pay continues. I would not say the job is safe until the roster is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd learn the mine's AI parts-ordering tool on a paid shift if the stores team introduces it. I'd compare its suggestions with actual pipe failures for a month. If Blue Mesa cuts my hours, I'd apply for a drainage lead post at another nearby mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The family could absorb a cut, but I would still miss the income and the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust a remote pump?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to see the pressure records through at least one heavy storm and inspect the joints afterward. A dry-weather demonstration would tell me little. Once the evidence is there, I can work with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you volunteer for a controls course immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would wait until the first operator has used the system in real weather. Then I would take a paid course if the mine has a post attached. I am willing to learn after a proper trial, not a sales pitch.

say: I would ask for a **storm trial** before trusting a remote pump.
I would explain that **orders and callouts** change before hands-on pipe work.
think: Some **lead hours** could shrink, though clinic income and other mines give us options.
I would not call the **roster secure** until the mine shows its plan.
do: Learn the **AI ordering tool** on a paid shift if introduced this year.
Compare **pipe suggestions** with failures and apply nearby if Blue Mesa cuts hours.
feel: **Anxious** about possible income loss, with a strong household buffer.
S1.quote: A dry-weather demonstration would tell me little.
fieldNote: Her **adoption threshold** is one heavy storm and inspected joints, not a polished demonstration.
She treats **other mine posts** as possibilities rather than promised work.

steps.text: Learn the AI parts-ordering tool on a paid shift if introduced
Apply for nearby drainage lead work if Blue Mesa cuts hours
Compare AI pipe suggestions with actual failures for one month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2028 could handle rainfall planning and parts orders quickly, while capable hands-on robots follow around 2031. I would ask Blue Mesa for separate plans for the office and pump crews. I would tell colleagues to get the actual roster before assuming a date for a layoff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 when thinking AI changes planning and 63 at the robot date, two years before I hope to stop. My lead planning duties might disappear early, and the truck work might go later. We have savings and Victor's wage, but I would not like drawing down retirement money for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the retirement office for written estimates at 63 and 65 this month. I'd cancel the planned patio work and put its budget into cash savings. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for a drainage role at a nearby pit if an actual vacancy opens and watch any pump robot trial before signing up for new controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with choices. The threat reaches my pay, though our savings give me time to compare a job offer with early retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would decide between another mine and stopping early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Victor and I would compare the posted wage and travel time with the written retirement estimate. A nearby job has to be worth the extra years of callouts. I would not leave on the basis of a machine brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is the patio budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We set aside about five thousand for paving and drainage at home. I would keep it in cash until the mine's staffing plan is clear. The patio can wait for the next summer.

say: I would mark **2028 planning** changes and the separate 2031 hands-on robot risk.
I would ask for **crew rosters** before assuming anyone has lost a job.
think: My **lead duties** could shrink at 60 and physical pump work around 63.
Our **savings and clinic wage** buy time, but two lost mine years would reduce retirement choices.
do: Cancel the **patio work** and move its five-thousand budget into cash savings.
Get **retirement estimates** and apply for a posted nearby drainage vacancy after 2028.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible two-year wage gap, with options to check.
S2.quote: I would not leave on the basis of a machine brochure.
fieldNote: She compares **travel and pay** with the actual retirement estimate before choosing another mine.
The **patio budget** becomes a cash reserve, with no claim that money alone covers two years.

steps.text: Cancel the planned home patio project this month
Apply for a posted nearby drainage role after 2028
Request pension estimates at 63 and 65 before choosing retirement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2031 could handle pump schedules while capable hands-on robots follow around 2034. That gives the crew five years to learn the controls if a proper trial works. I would ask for pressure logs and paid training places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when planning changes and 66 at the robot date. If my work and retirement figures hold, I can stop at 65 before the physical pump work changes. A cut in lead hours at 63 could still reduce the last two years of pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add one hundred and fifty a month to our retirement account from now, while the high wage holds. I'd take a paid remote pump course this year if the first storm trial passes and a real operator post is attached. In the first year after 2031, if lead planning goes, I'd take a regular pump shift if it pays enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. There is a likely path to 65, but I would want the shift offer in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is enough pay on a regular shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Victor and I would compare the monthly offer with our bills and retirement contribution. I could accept a lower title, but not a surprise cut that defeats the point of working two more years. I would check the payslip terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why learn remote controls if you may stop at 65?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid course could protect the last two years of work, provided the storm trial proves the pump. I would not use retirement savings for a speculative certificate. I like learning a proven system.

say: I would seek **storm logs** and paid training tied to real operator posts.
I would separate **2031 schedules** from the 2034 hands-on robot date.
think: I might stop at **65** before pump robots arrive if wages and retirement figures hold.
A **lead-hours cut** at 63 could still affect two years of income.
do: Add **one hundred fifty** monthly to retirement savings while high pay continues.
Take a **paid controls course** after a passed storm trial and accept a bill-covering pump shift if offered.
feel: **Anxious** about final working years, despite a likely bridge.
S3.quote: I would not use retirement savings for a speculative certificate.
fieldNote: Her **course decision** depends on a passed trial, pay and an attached real post.
She checks **payslip terms** before trading lead duties for a regular pump shift.

steps.text: Add one hundred fifty monthly to retirement savings while pay holds
Take paid remote pump training if a storm trial passes and a post exists
Take a regular pump shift after 2031 if offered at bill-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade allows time for proper wet-weather tests and training for younger pump crews. AGI by 2036 could take schedules, and capable hands-on robots follow around 2039. I would ask the mine to publish the storm records each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 in 2036 and 71 when robots reach the physical work. If Victor and I can afford the planned stop at 65, neither date threatens my mine wage. I would still care about the people who need a pump job after I leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the drainage crew this year and add one hundred and fifty a month to retirement savings if our budget permits. I'd get the retirement estimate at 65 in writing and review it with Victor. In the first year after 2036, if retired, I'd offer occasional advice on old pit drainage maps when the new crew asks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own income if the account supports stopping at 65. I would stay interested in whether the mine keeps safe water routes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change the stopping age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the written retirement estimate does not cover our bills, I would stay on a little longer if health and shifts allow. The hands-on robot date is later, so there is room to adjust. I would make the call with Victor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach the new crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the new crew where water collects after a sideways storm and how the old maps miss a low corner. They can compare that with their new tools. I would not pretend my memory is better than a measured level.

say: I would ask for **published storm tests** and training before the 2036 and 2039 changes.
I would help younger workers learn **pit drainage** from measurements and older maps.
think: My **planned stop at 65** comes before either technology date if retirement income covers our bills.
The younger crew still faces **longer job risk** after I leave.
do: Keep **leading drainage shifts** and add one hundred fifty monthly to retirement savings if affordable.
Review a **written retirement estimate** with Victor this year.
feel: **Calm** about my own income if the account supports retirement.
S4.quote: I would not pretend my memory is better than a measured level.
fieldNote: Her **retirement plan** depends on written figures, not the scenario alone.
She would pass on **drainage knowledge** while accepting that new measurements can correct her memory.

steps.text: Keep leading Blue Mesa drainage shifts this year
Add one hundred fifty monthly to retirement savings if affordable

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the lead planning could change at 60 and the pump truck around 63, two years before I hope to stop. A published staffing plan, a real nearby vacancy and clear retirement figures would help us choose. We have time to decide, but I want facts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who goes out in a storm to check a pipe joint after a remote pump stops. I can learn good controls, but a screen cannot tighten a loose coupling. The mine will need a named person for the wet work.

headlineQuote: The mine will need a named person for the wet work.
portrait: **Aisha Garcia**, 58, leads drainage work at a large open pit mine and operates a heavy pump truck herself.
Her **high mine pay**, strong savings, partner’s clinic wage and several nearby pits support a planned stop around 65.
She uses **AI occasionally** for rain tables and adopts remote tools after real storm tests prove them.
The **fastest AGI** picture risks two working years; slower dates allow measured training, savings and a possible shift bridge.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could affect planning at 60 and hands-on pump work around 63, ahead of her planned stop.
whatWouldHelp: A **published staffing plan**, an available nearby vacancy and clear retirement figures would help her choose.
